summary: Root cause (confidence: medium, 0.62): the pricing-engine experiment flag cfg-3120 — flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5 -> 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z — enabled a CPU-heavy code path for all traffic, driving pricing-engine CPU from ~38-40% to 98-100% and p99 latency from ~60ms to ~2534ms in the very next 60s bucket, which pushed order-service quote calls past their 2500ms timeout from 12:06:10Z onward. The fault originates in pricing-engine's compute cost under the fully-rolled-out flagged code path; the fix target is reverting/disengaging cfg-3120 or fixing that path. Alternatives are excluded by positive evidence, not dismissal: H2 (market-data-service protobuf deploy at 11:56Z) by pricing-engine CPU/latency being flat at baseline for the 15 minutes spanning that deploy and stepping only at 12:05 plus market-data-service emitting zero WARN+ logs; H3 (redis-cache) by healthy/flat hit-ratio, CPU, evictions and clients at onset; H4 (capacity/organic load) by flat request_rate across onset. The one unproven hop is the mechanism detail that the Greeks v2 path is materially more CPU-intensive and behaves near-on/off at full rollout — this caps confidence, and the ~2h no-recovery/no-revert signature is treated as part of the same origin rather than a separate one.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Greeks v2 feature-flag ramp to 100% saturates pricing-engine CPU (with persistent-cost mechanism folded in)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Config change cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 on pricing-engine at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, enabling the CPU-heavy Greeks v2 computation for all traffic. pricing-engine CPU steps 38%->98.65% and p99 steps ~60ms->2534ms in the very next 60s bucket (12:05:00Z). Order quotes served by pricing-engine then exceed order-service's 2500ms timeout, producing continuous quote timeouts from 12:06:10Z. Fault originates in pricing-engine's compute cost under the newly fully-rolled-out code path, triggered by the flag change. The persistence detail (flat 98-100% CPU and flat ~2.6s p99 with no downslope and no visible revert through 13:59Z) is treated as an assumption about the flagged code path's cost profile (self-sustaining/near-on-off at full rollout), not as a separate origin: same origin, same fix target (revert/disengage cfg-3120 or fix the flagged path), so it is not split into a competing hypothesis.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 on pricing-engine at 12:04:00Z, 12 min before the report
Greeks v2 path becomes active for 100% of traffic and is materially more CPU-expensive (and cost does not scale linearly back down with partial rollout; near-on/off at full rollout)
pricing-engine CPU saturates 38%->98.65% in the 12:05:00Z bucket, one 60s bucket after the ramp
pricing-engine p99 steps from ~60ms to ~2500-2850ms at 12:05:00Z, one minute before the first order-service timeout
Saturation is CPU-bound: memory flat ~46-53%
order-service -> pricing-engine (http) quote call exceeds the 2500ms timeout; first error 12:06:10Z, step-change not ramp, continuous to 13:58:24Z
Saturation persists with no recovery and no revert and restarts=0 through 13:59Z (consistent with flag remaining applied; the flagged path's cost is sustained)

assumptions: The newly enabled Greeks v2 code path is materially more CPU-intensive than Greeks v1

Its cost does not scale proportionally down with rollout_pct, or it engages a self-sustaining/hot loop at full rollout, which is why the flat 98-100% CPU shows no downslope (mechanism detail, not a separate origin)

The 12:04:00Z flag write propagated to pricing-engine within ~1 minute and drove the 12:05 CPU/latency step; sub-minute resolution is unavailable (F31), so this is inference-by-alignment at one 60s bucket

The flag remains applied (no revert) so the CPU cost stays applied continuously through 13:59Z; the absence of a revert record is inferred from zero pricing-engine log matches (F27) and restarts=0 (F28), not from the config-audit store

ranked_hypotheses.title: Persistent post-ramp state: flag-ramp change but no self-recovery (mechanically incomplete H1)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Same origin as H1 (cfg-3120 flag ramp at 12:04Z enabling an expensive code path) but acknowledging that the saturation shows NO recovery and NO revert for ~2 hours (F25/F26/F30, restarts=0 F28). For an ordinary feature-flag toggle whose cost scales with rollout_pct, restoring the flag would restore CPU; the flat 98-100% CPU and flat 2.6s p99 with no downslope indicates the new code path either introduced a self-sustaining state (a runaway/loop or a hot path that cannot complete) or is genuinely order-of-magnitude more expensive and gated purely as on/off at the 100% boundary. This framing treats the no-recovery signature as part of the originating defect triggered by the flag change rather than a discrepancy.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps the greeks_v2 flag 5->100 at 12:04:00Z
The newly 100%-active code path holds pricing-engine CPU at 98-100% indefinitely (no ramp-down), latent until full rollout
p99 stays flat at ~2.4-2.85s with no downslope through 13:58Z; CPU mean 98.96, p99 mean 2633ms
No feature-flag revert is visible in pricing-engine logs over 12:16-13:59Z and restarts=0
order-service quote timeouts continue from 12:06:10Z to 13:58:24Z

assumptions: The absence of recovery is attributable to the flag remaining applied (no revert) rather than to the flag being irrelevant
The new code path is a persistent consume, not a bursty one

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf change (dep-6111) slowed the pricing path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Deployment dep-6111 switched market-data-service quote serialization to protobuf at 11:56:00Z. The reporter suspects the changed serialization raised payload/CPU cost for a downstream consumer (pricing-engine), driving pricing-engine CPU/latency and thus order quote timeouts. Fault originates in market-data-service's v5.2.0 release; it stays applied (live, not rolled back), which would be consistent with the ~2h flat, non-recovering saturation. Kept active because its mechanism (protobuf slower for the downstream parser) was never directly tested — it is contradicted only indirectly.

causal_chain.claim: dep-6111 market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed 11:56:00Z, status live, rolled_back_at null
protobuf serialization is more CPU-expensive for a downstream parser (pricing-engine)
pricing-engine, downstream of market-data-service on the quote path, sees CPU and latency rise
order-service quote timeouts follow from 12:06:10Z

assumptions: The serialization change alone raises CPU cost enough to saturate pricing-engine
A 9-minute quiet gap (11:56 deploy vs 12:05 onset) is plausible for a format-effect that builds over time
The mechanism is untested: no parser-cost/latency measurement for the new protobuf path exists in the evidence

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation stalls the quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache is shared and an inbound dependency of both pricing-engine and market-data-service on the quote path, so a failover/cold-cache/saturation could stall pricing-engine and thus order quotes. This origin is REJECTED: direct cache-health metrics contradict every degradation signature at onset.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache is shared, inbound dependency of both pricing-engine and market-data-service on the quote path
redis-cache degrades at ~12:05Z
Contrary: hit_ratio_pct peaks (98.46), cpu 21-23% flat, evictions below baseline, clients/memory stable
pricing-engine latency -> ~2.5s and order-service timeouts follow

ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct redis-cache health metrics show no degradation at onset: hit_ratio high/peaking (F20), CPU flat 21-23% (F21), no eviction storm (F22), stable clients/memory (F23, all missing_points 0 per F24). The degraded component (pricing-engine) is CPU-saturated (F16/F17) while the shared cache is idle-healthy, so a shared-cache bottleneck is excluded by positive evidence, not mere inference. Residual caveat: redis-cache exposes no failover/error counter (F24), so an instantaneous failover cannot be read directly.

ranked_hypotheses.title: pricing-engine CPU saturation from organic market-open load (capacity)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Precedent HIST-113 shows pricing-engine CPU saturating at market open causing quote timeouts; if this were the same recurring capacity pattern, a load surge would saturate pricing-engine CPU at 12:05Z independent of any change. REJECTED: pricing-engine request_rate is flat across onset and the whole window, so no load surge coincided with the 12:05 CPU step.

causal_chain.claim: HIST-113 precedent: pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open -> quote timeouts/cpu 99%
An organic load surge saturates pricing-engine CPU at 12:05Z
Contrary: request_rate is flat at onset and across the window, no surge

ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: pricing-engine request_rate is flat at and around onset (F19: 12:04=623.49, 12:05=623.49, min 590.66 max 687.48) and flat across the full window (F29), so there is no load surge to attribute the CPU step to. The capacity_saturation precedent HIST-113 is not matched.

facts.statement: cfg-3120 on pricing-engine ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'); this was the only config change across all services in the window, from a full retried config-audit query.

pricing-engine CPU_pct was flat at 38-42% from 11:50Z through 12:04Z (including every minute after the 11:56Z deploy) and then stepped to 98.65% at 12:05:00Z and 99.25% at 12:06:00Z, coincident with the latency jump.
pricing-engine p99 latency was flat at ~57-62ms from 11:50Z through 12:04Z (including 11:56Z) and stepped to 2534.9ms at 12:05:00Z and 2521.4ms at 12:06:00Z.

order-service quote timeouts began at 12:06:10Z with the first ERROR log 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms orderId=4bd44879'; all 225 matched ERROR entries are the same timeout pattern and errors run continuously through 13:58:24Z.

pricing-engine memory_pct stayed flat ~46-53% across onset, so the failure is CPU-bound, not a memory/leak symptom.

pricing-engine request_rate showed no load surge at 12:05Z (12:04=623.49, 12:05=623.49, min 590.66 / max 687.48) and remained flat ~571-741 req/s across the whole window, excluding an organic market-open load surge.

redis-cache health was normal/healthy at onset: hit_ratio_pct 12:04=95.76, 12:05=98.46 (peaking, not degrading); cpu_pct flat 21.16-23.09%; evictions_per_min 2.15-3.76 (below the 12:00-12:03 baseline); connected_clients stable 296.5-335.37 and memory_pct 66.95-72.72%.
market-data-service emitted zero WARN-or-higher logs in 11:45-13:59Z (total_matched 0) with data range covering 08:00-13:59Z, despite the report attributing the change to it.

pricing-engine cpu_pct never recovered in 12:16-13:59Z (180s buckets, min 97.76, max 100.0, mean 98.96) and latency_p99_ms stayed ~2391-2844ms (mean 2633.34) with no downslope.

No revert/rollback signal for cfg-3120 or the greeks_v2 flag appears in pricing-engine logs (queries for 'flag', 'cfg-3120', 'greeks_v2', 'rollback' over 12:16-13:59Z each returned 0 matches) and pricing-engine restarts stayed 0 for the entire 12:16-13:59Z window.
All pricing-engine metric readings used here have missing_points 0, so the flat-baseline and step readings are real data, not MISSING/null placeholders.

Sub-minute resolution is unavailable for pricing-engine: cpu_pct at max_points=32 and 48 and error_rate at max_points=40 all returned bucket_seconds=60, so onset cannot be pinned below one 60s bucket.

Quote-path topology: order-service -> pricing-engine (http) -> market-data-service (http); pricing-engine is a direct, non-shared dependency of order-service, and redis-cache is the shared component common to both pricing-engine and market-data-service.
No deployments or config changes were found scoped to order-service (market-data-scoped deploy query returned only dep-6111; order-service config query returned count 0).

Its cost does not scale proportionally down with rollout_pct, or it engages a self-sustaining/hot loop at full rollout, which is why flat 98-100% CPU shows no downslope through 13:59Z (mechanism detail, not a separate origin).
The 12:04:00Z flag write propagated to pricing-engine within ~1 minute and drove the 12:05 step; sub-minute resolution is unavailable, so this is inference-by-alignment at one 60s bucket.

recommended_actions.action: Revert / disengage cfg-3120 on pricing-engine: set flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct back to its pre-incident value (5) or disable the greeks_v2 flag for pricing-engine, and confirm the change landed in the config-audit store.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only pricing-engine-relevant change and its 12:04Z write is immediately followed by the CPU step to 98.65% and p99 step to 2534.9ms; the flagged code path is the identified compute-cost origin, so removing it is the direct mitigation.

recommended_actions.action: Verify recovery after the flag change: watch pricing-engine cpu_pct and latency_p99_ms return toward the ~40% / ~60ms baseline and confirm order-service quote-timeout ERROR logs stop and error_rate returns to ~0.2; note that if CPU/latency stay flat at 98-100%/~2.6s after the flag write lands, escalate to restarting pricing-engine as the next mitigation.
recommended_actions.rationale: The window shows no spontaneous recovery or revert (flat 98-100% CPU and ~2.6s p99 through 13:59Z, restarts 0, no revert log), so recovery must be actively confirmed; a non-response to revert would distinguish the persistent-state variant H5 from a simple flag-cost revert.

recommended_actions.action: As a safety net if revert does not restore pricing-engine within a few minutes, restart the pricing-engine process (restarts were 0 throughout, so no clear has been attempted) and confirm CPU/p99 normalization.
recommended_actions.rationale: The saturation is a hard CPU-bound state with no downslope and no process restart in the window; if the flagged path left a self-sustaining state, a process cycle is the cheap way to clear it.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back dep-6111 (market-data-service v5.2.0 protobuf quote serialization) only if the flag revert does not restore pricing-engine CPU/latency; keep it as a held-down candidate rather than the first action.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 remains the only live alternative with an untested mechanism (protobuf slower for the downstream parser) and the deploy remains live with rolled_back_at null; the flat-then-step shape spanning 11:56Z and market-data-service's silent logs make it unlikely, but a rollback is the decisive test if revert fails.

recommended_actions.action: Measure the CPU/latency cost of the Greeks v2 code path directly (bench or load test at rollout_pct 0 vs 100) and fix the expensive path or gate it behind capacity-based rollout rather than a binary full-rollout default.
recommended_actions.rationale: The single unproven hop in the conclusion is the mechanism — that Greeks v2 is materially more CPU-intensive and behaves near-on/off at full rollout; measuring it converts an assumption into evidence and confirms the fix.

recommended_actions.action: Add guardrails for experiment/config ramps: staged rollout with automatic rollback driven by pricing-engine CPU/p99 SLOs (e.g. halt and revert if cpu_pct > 90% or p99 > 500ms for >1 minute after a ramp), plus alerting on experiment-ramp writes to CPU-bound services.
recommended_actions.rationale: A 5 -> 100 single-step ramp on a CPU-heavy path took pricing-engine to full saturation within one 60s bucket with no automatic detection or revert for ~2 hours (no revert signals, restarts 0).

recommended_actions.action: Increase pricing-engine metric resolution and add order-service/quote-path SLO alerting tied to pricing-engine p99, so sub-minute onset attribution and fast detection are possible in future.
recommended_actions.rationale: Sub-minute resolution is unavailable (60s buckets floor even at high max_points), which is the main reason onset attribution cannot be tightened below one minute, and the incident ran ~2h before the report.

data_gaps: First config-audit call was partial (shard 2/3 did not respond); changes between 10:00-11:00Z and shard-2-only entries remain unverified, so an additional earlier config change cannot be fully excluded.

No live trace/end-to-end tool was available, so the order-service quote timeout could not be attributed to a specific span and the deploy-vs-ramp onset could not be discriminated below 60s resolution.

The config-audit store was not re-queried for a 12:16-13:59Z revert record; revert-freeness rests on pricing-engine log queries (0 matches) and restarts=0, which could miss a change recorded only in the audit store.
order-service cpu_pct / memory_pct / db_pool_in_use at the onset minute were not queried, so it is not confirmed whether order-service was purely a downstream victim or had local saturation.
Only the top 40 of 225 order-service ERROR logs were returned (truncated), so a second, later error signature after 12:25:54Z cannot be ruled out.
No latency/error metrics were pulled for market-data-service or other quote-path hops besides pricing-engine and order-service, so 'localized vs systemic' rests on partial coverage.
redis-cache exposes no failover/error-counter metric, so an instantaneous failover cannot be read directly; the H3 exclusion relies on the four healthy health metrics.
No shared library node appears in the dependency graph, so it cannot be confirmed at runtime whether order-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service share a protobuf/serialization library.
No historical precedent was retrieved specifically for feature-flag-ramp-induced latency regressions, so that precedent class is unverified.

The order-service error_rate query for 12:16-13:59Z was not executed, so ongoing order-service failure to the end of the window is corroborated only by pricing-engine saturation and the continuous ERROR logs.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: pricing-engine CPU and p99 returning to baseline promptly after reverting/disengaging cfg-3120 would confirm H1 as the root cause (and rule out a self-sustaining state).
pricing-engine CPU/latency restoring to baseline only after rolling back dep-6111 (with the flag revert not helping) would shift the root cause to H2 (protobuf serialization change).

Evidence of an earlier or additional config/deploy change in the unread shard-2 audit window (or a change type other than deployment/config) aligning with the 12:05Z step would reopen the origin question.
A metric showing a load surge or a request-rate/complexity increase on pricing-engine at 12:05Z would revive H4 (capacity/organic load).
A redis-cache failover/error event at 12:04-12:06Z (from a source exposing failover counters) would revive H3.
Evidence that the cessation of order-service timeouts coincides with something other than pricing-engine recovery (e.g. an order-service timeout/config change) would challenge the causal chain.
Failure to reproduce the CPU step in a controlled run of the Greeks v2 path at rollout_pct=100 would falsify the assumed mechanism and re-open the origin attribution.
